newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan may face tougher task managing forex policy.
newsitem.headline: Japan may face tougher task managing forex policy.

text.p: Japan's policy-makers are likely to find it increasingly difficult to use their past tactics of market intervention and "talking down" the dollar to curb its rise against the yen, dealers say.

This is because of outside calls for a stronger dollar by Japan's Group of Seven (G7) European allies, who are trying to boost their exports and strengthen their economies ready for monetary union, they say.

"The Ministry (of Finance) may find it difficult to resort to the option of dollar-selling intervention if the dollar advances further into the 115-120 yen range," said Shinichiro Maruyama, head of spot trading at the Industrial Bank of Japan (IBJ) Ltd.
European government officials, such as French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, have repeatedly called for a higher dollar.
Their plea reflects a strong desire to boost their exports and balance their budgets in a bid to meet tough criteria for membership in the European Union's single currency, to be launched in 1999.
"There is a risk that a dollar rise might spin out of control for the (Japan's Finance) Ministry," said Kazunori Iida, manager at the foreign exchange department at Nissho Iwai Corp.
"The economy is not so good. Interest rates won't go up. These views on fundamentals have spurred a flow of Japanese capital into overseas markets and pushed the dollar up," he added.

On Friday, the dollar rose to a level at which even Eisuke Sakakibara, an influential Finance Ministry official dubbed "Mr Yen" for his role in driving up the dollar from last year's postwar low, showed discomfort.
Asked on Friday about the dollar's recent recovery, Sakakibara bluntly replied: "I won't talk about currencies".
Earlier this month, the dollar dived against the yen after Sakakibara said the economy was stronger than the market believed, suggesting the one-way weakening of the yen was about to run its course.

But aggressive demand for dollars from Japanese operators flared up again after the Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan" survey released on Wednesday showed only a slight improvement in corporate sentiment and continued uncertainty about the future of the economy.
This convinced operators that Japan's ultra low interest rates would continue and encouraged Japanese investors to beef up their investments overseas in a bid for higher yields.
There are also worries about more failures of small Japanese banks, dealers say.

"There is no guarantee that the dollar will stay tamely in a range of 110-115 yen which the authorities might favour," said IBJ's Maruyama. He said the dollar may reach 116 yen by the end of this year.
"The ministry will not be able to keep putting the brake on the dollar's rise by words so often," he added.
The dollar stood at around 113.50 yen in late afternoon trade on Friday after rising as high as 113.92 yen in the morning on what dealers said was simply a lack of reasons to buy the yen.

A weak yen helps Japanese exporters but also holds the risk that trade friction with the United States could erupt at any time due to an expected fall in domestic demand in Japan and a possible slowdown in the U.S. economy next year.
Sakakibara was seen as the key person in helping to drive the dollar up above 100 yen last year by hammering out a package of deregulation measures and aggressive dollar buying intervention.
But dealers say the dollar has risen in recent months without any help from Japanese officials, responding instead to market forces.
